young.html: Hegel was a German professor who told the whole history of the world as one big story. In his story, the hero is not a king or a general. The hero is an idea: freedom.

Long ago, Hegel said, people thought only the king was free. Later, in ancient Greece and Rome, some people were free and others were slaves. Over many centuries, people came to believe that every person is meant to be free. That idea took a long time to turn into laws, and it is still being worked out.

young.cap: Hegel's four stages, from "one is free" to "all are free." Tap each one.

young.html: For parents: Hegel's picture of Asia and Africa was badly mistaken, as later historians have shown. The lesson says so, and it is a good chance to talk about how people judge cultures they do not know well.

Your own history book. Draw a timeline of your life so far with five events. Then give it a theme, the way Hegel did: is your story about growing braver, kinder, more independent? Which events fit the theme, and which do not?

full.html: Hegel (1770–1831) lectured on the philosophy of world history five times at the University of Berlin, from 1822 to 1831. After his death, his student Eduard Gans and later his son Karl put the lectures together from Hegel's own notes and students' notebooks, and published them in 1837. J. Sibree's English translation followed in 1857.

Hegel begins by sorting historians. Original historians, like Herodotus and Thucydides, wrote about events they lived through. Reflective historians look back and arrange the past, sometimes to draw lessons, which Hegel doubts anyone learns. Philosophical history, his own kind, looks for the reason running through it all.

full.text: But what experience and history teach is this,—that peoples and governments never have learned anything from history, or acted on principles deduced from it.
full.author: Hegel
full.work: Lectures on the Philosophy of History, Introduction

full.text: The History of the world is none other than the progress of the consciousness of Freedom.
full.author: Hegel
full.work: Lectures on the Philosophy of History, Introduction

full.html: Hegel divides world history into stages, in a famous formula: the Eastern nations knew only that one is free; the Greek and Roman world, that some are free; and the modern Christian world, that all are free, as human beings.

full.name: gb-hegel-history
full.cap: Hegel's stages, with our notes on how later historians judge them.

full.html: Hegel was trying to show that history is not "one thing after another" but has a direction. That idea, that history is going somewhere, shaped a great deal of 19th-century thought, from Marx to many believers in progress.

full.text: Passion and the cunning of reason

full.html: How does freedom move forward if people act for selfish reasons? Hegel answers that great figures, his world-historical individuals such as Alexander, Caesar and Napoleon, chase their own ambitions, and yet without meaning to they carry history's purpose forward. He calls this the cunning of reason.

full.text: ... we may affirm absolutely that nothing great in the World has been accomplished without passion.
full.author: Hegel
full.work: Lectures on the Philosophy of History, Introduction

full.html: Taking Hegel's stages as a fair account of the world's peoples. His picture of China, India and Africa rested on the thin and often prejudiced reports available in Europe in the 1820s, and historians reject it. His lectures are read today for their big idea about freedom, not as a reliable history of those places.

deep.text: Is there a direction to history?

deep.html: Hegel's lectures raised a question every later philosopher of history had to face. Marx kept Hegel's stages but said the engine is economic, not Spirit. Tolstoy, in War and Peace (later on this ladder), mocked the idea that great men steer history. Nietzsche doubted that history has any goal at all. Many 20th-century historians grew wary of any grand pattern, after seeing what was done in the name of history's supposed direction; others still find the idea of a long, uneven growth of freedom worth arguing about.

items: Does history have a direction, or is that a story we tell afterward?
Do great individuals make history, or does history make them?
Can good come out of selfish actions? Can you think of an example?
How should we judge a thinker whose big idea is inspiring but whose facts were wrong?

deep.html: Compare Herodotus and Thucydides, Hegel's "original" historians, earlier on this ladder, and Gibbon, a great "reflective" one.

questions: Hegel said nothing great is done without passion. What are you passionate about?
Do you think people learn from history? Can you think of a time someone did, or did not?
Who is someone in history who changed the world? Did they mean to?
What does it mean for everyone to be free? Is that true in every country today?
Hegel was wrong about many peoples he never studied. How can we avoid judging others without knowing them?
